claims.text: Low hardness and strength in equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi arise from its stable single-phase solid-solution state.
The single-phase state of CoCrFeNiTi promotes easy and homogeneous dislocation glide.
Deformation of the stated CoCrFeNiTi state occurs without significant dislocation pile-up.
Deformation of the stated CoCrFeNiTi state occurs without significant twinning or phase transformation.
Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has low lattice distortion.
Microstructural simplicity and low lattice distortion suppress the formation of deformation barriers that would otherwise strengthen the alloy.
The initial material is homogeneous, single phase, and contains minimal secondary phases or precipitates.
Controlled pre-straining followed by annealing, or a small alloying change, can promote deformation-induced twinning or a limited phase transformation in CoCrFeNiTi.
The controlled comparison is between as-cast and thermomechanically processed samples tested by room-temperature uniaxial tension and nanoindentation.
The relevant structural mediator is the density and distribution of mobile dislocations and the absence or presence of deformation twins or transformation products.
Few impediments in the simple solid solution cause deformation to be accommodated primarily by unobstructed dislocation glide.
Deformation-induced twinning or phase transformation typically introduces additional obstacles and work-hardening.
The absence of strain-induced twinning or phase transformation keeps yield strength and hardness low while permitting favorable plasticity.
Processing that triggers twinning or a limited phase transformation should increase hardness and yield strength relative to the as-cast state.
Processed samples should exhibit new twins, transformation products, or secondary-phase particles detectable by microscopy.
The newly produced twins, transformation products, or secondary-phase particles impede dislocation motion.
As-cast single-phase CoCrFeNiTi combines favorable plasticity and machinability with relatively low hardness and strength.

The hypothesis is limited to equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi tested at room temperature under quasi-static uniaxial loading or nanoindentation, without significant secondary-phase precipitates or grain-boundary segregation.
The magnitude of strengthening and the role of Ti in lattice distortion or phase stability are not quantified.
Failure to observe increased hardness and yield strength after processing would falsify the proposed strengthening mechanism.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome allows secondary-phase particles as the strengthening feature, whereas the stated boundary requires the microstructure to remain free of significant secondary-phase precipitates. It is unclear whether deformation products are exempt from this boundary.
